newsitem.title: USA: New York trial lawyers take aim at "Sammy the Bull".
newsitem.headline: New York trial lawyers take aim at "Sammy the Bull".

text.p: Attorneys introduced documents into the trial of a reputed Genovese crime family boss on Friday that sought to discredit former mob hitman and government witness Salvatore "Sammy the Bull" Gravano.

Defence attorney Michael Marinaccio said the documents showed Gravano split $850,000 with author Peter Maas for their book, "Underboss," published in April. He said the documents also revealed that Gravano had additional deals, such as a $10,000 payment to do a voice-over for a TV advertisement.
Gravano testified on Thursday that he was paid $250,000 for the memoir of his life as a mobster, expected royalties and wanted $1 million for any movie deal.
A lawyer for Maas and the publisher, HarperCollins, denied that Gravano received any money for the book.
Under New York law, Gravano is not allowed to make money from an account of his crimes, which included 19 murders.

On the second day of his testimony in the murder and racketeering trial of Vincent "The Chin" Gigante, Gravano defiantly vowed to fight attempts by relatives of his murder victims to recover money he made from the best seller.

During 1 1/2 days of questioning by Gigante's attorney in Brooklyn Federal Court, Gravano pointed to Gigante as the head of the Genovese crime family but did not link him directly to the seven murders the indictment accuses him of ordering.
The 21-count indictment accuses Gigante of ordering the killing of seven people and conspiring to kill three others, allegedly to avenge breaches of Mafia protocol such as unauthorised slayings.
Gigante's attorneys say he has been incapacitated by mental illness for years, but prosecutors say he has feigned illness to avoid prosecution.

Gravano was arrested in 1990 and opted to cooperate with the government rather than face life in prison. He spent five years in jail and has left the federal witness protection programme but remains in hiding.
Gravano's testimony helped convict reputed Godfather John Gotti in 1992. He confessed to 19 murders as part of his deal with the government to testify against reputed mobsters for at least two years.
Hammering away at Gravano's ability to tell the truth, Marinaccio recalled advice Gravano gave his former mob partners on evading and lying in court.
Marinaccio quoted Gravano as having said the mob was "all lies ... It's one doublecross after another, one scheme after another and one betrayal after another."
